sources.entry: Profiling a warehouse-scale computer - Fleet counter profile showing services stall on instruction fetch and burn cycles in shared routines, which SPEC lacks.

summary.title: Profiling a warehouse-scale computer
summary.one_liner: Learn how a longitudinal, fleet-wide hardware-counter study of Google's live datacenter jobs shows diverse workloads, a large "datacenter tax" of shared low-level routines, and front-end and cache bottlenecks that SPEC-style benchmarks miss.
keywords: how do datacenter workloads stall the cpu
why spec does not represent servers
takeaways: Production datacenter workloads are very diverse, with no single application dominating cycles; the hottest binary accounts for about 10% and about 50 binaries cover roughly 60%.
Roughly 22-27% of cycles go to 'datacenter tax' (protobufs, RPC, hashing, compression, allocation, memmove), making these shared routines candidates for hardware acceleration.
Front-end stalls account for 15-30% of pipeline slots and instruction-cache pressure is a major bottleneck, while memory latency matters more than bandwidth.
The study uses random sampling via GWP and Intel Ivy Bridge performance counters with Top-Down cycle accounting over about 20,000 machines and three years.
summary.summary: The paper presents a microarchitectural profile of live jobs on more than 20,000 Google machines over about three years, collected with low-overhead random sampling (GWP) and Intel Ivy Bridge performance counters. It analyzes workload diversity across binaries and leaf functions, then identifies a 'datacenter tax' of common low-level routines such as protobufs, RPC, hashing, compression, allocation, and memmove. Using the Top-Down method to measure stall cycles, it reports front-end and instruction-cache bottlenecks, data-cache-dominated stalls, latency over bandwidth, and limited SMT benefits. It is a research paper (ISCA 2015) rather than a tutorial.
